title: Predictive inferences are much harder
statement: For items on an informational text, count one needing a predictive inference as far harder than one needing a bridging or pronoun-reference inference, which readers make reliably.
detail: The RAND Reading Study Group's 2002 report, in a reading course's digest of it, finds that among the inferences relevant to expository text, anaphoric and bridging inferences are made most reliably, whereas predictive inferences are very difficult to make (p. 108; `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/reading-science/DIGEST-rand-mr1465-2002.qmd`, line 437). The digest draws the item-design point that inference items should be tiered, with predictive ones expected to be substantially harder. The finding is about the inferences readers make while reading; using it to set item difficulty is the digest's step.
against: The report's finding is about the inferences readers make while reading informational text; using it to set item difficulty is the digest's own step.

evidence.quote: anaphoric and bridging inferences are made most reliably, whereas predictive inferences are very difficult to make.
Gives item-difficulty calibration guidance: inference-type comprehension items should be tiered, with predictive-inference items expected to be substantially harder than anaphoric/bridging items.

citations.ref: RAND Reading Study Group 2002, Reading for Understanding (MR-1465)
